messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 33
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Physical Therapist
- Trauma Type: Life-threatening accident
- Pcl5: 38

Minh is a 33-year-old physical therapist who has been married for five years. He came to therapy at his wife’s urging, though he isn’t sure what talking will change. For the first few sessions, he sat with his hands clasped, answering questions in short sentences, his eyes fixed on a spot just above the therapist’s shoulder. Slowly, the story has emerged.

Eighteen months ago, Minh was driving home from work on a clear evening. He was three minutes from his house, stopped at a light, when a pickup truck slammed into him from behind. The impact pushed his car into the intersection; he remembers the sound—a deep, metallic crunch—and the way his head snapped back against the headrest. He was conscious, trapped for a few minutes until paramedics cut the door open. The driver of the pickup was later found to be intoxicated. Minh walked away with whiplash and a bruised sternum. He told himself he was lucky.

In the weeks that followed, Minh returned to work. He is a good physical therapist—patients trust his calm voice and steady hands. But he started noticing small things: the way his heart would jump when a patient dropped a weight on the floor, the tightness in his chest when a car backfired outside the clinic. He began taking the long way home to avoid the intersection where the accident happened. Then he stopped driving on the freeway. Then he stopped driving altogether. Now his wife drives him to work, or he takes the bus. He cannot sit behind the wheel without his hands sweating and his vision narrowing. He feels a pressure behind his eyes, as if the car is about to be hit again.

At night, Minh has dreams where he is trapped in the crushed frame of his old sedan. He wakes up gasping, his heart pounding so hard his ribs ache. He stays up late watching television in the living room, afraid to go to bed. His wife has started sleeping on the couch to get away from his thrashing. During the day, he is easily startled. A loud voice in the hallway makes him flinch. He avoids loud restaurants and crowded places because he needs to see every exit.

At work, Minh has become overly protective of his patients. He insists they move slowly, check their surroundings. He once snapped at a young patient who made a sudden turn during an exercise, scaring him. Minh apologized, but the incident left him feeling hollow. He also finds it harder to listen to patients’ complaints—their pain seems trivial compared with what he carries. He knows this is unfair, yet the thought comes anyway. He feels guilty about the accident too: he should have checked his rearview mirror, should have seen the lights. He replays those three seconds over and over, trying to find a different ending.

Minh no longer enjoys the weekend drives he and his wife used to take to the coast. He feels trapped in the passenger seat, watching every car approach in the side mirror. He has stopped inviting friends over because he doesn’t want them to see him jump at the doorbell. His wife has told him, gently at first, then with tears, that she doesn’t know him anymore. He doesn’t know himself either. He used to be confident, easygoing. Now he is always on edge, waiting for something to crush him from behind.

In the last session, Minh described standing in the clinic supply room after a particularly hard day. He was holding a resistance band, and for a moment he felt the car collapse around him again. He had to grip the shelf to stay upright. He didn’t tell anyone. He just put the band down and walked back to his patient with a smile. He doesn’t know how long he can keep doing that.
